synthesis.headline: Two Pacific systems seize the northern tier as the summer ridge splits; ensembles say the north-central trough, not a rebuilt interior ridge, wins the week
synthesis.narrative:
The organizing story today is a continent split along its middle, with the initiative passing to the northern tier. A deep, positively tilted 500 mb trough anchors the Pacific Northwest into British Columbia (axis near 564 dam), its tightly packed eastern flank implying a strong jet corridor draped from the northern Rockies toward the central Plains. At the surface that trough owns a cluster of weak lows (tightest 1000-1006 mb near the Washington-Oregon coast) and drives a sharp cold front south through the Rockies into the Desert Southwest, which carries the most organized isobar packing in the CONUS. Against that active West, a broad ridge over the central and southern Plains (588-591 dam) and a separate, more retrogressive eastern ridge from the Carolinas into Atlantic Canada (588-594 dam) keep the south and east warm and quiet. Between them a shortwave of slight negative tilt over the Ohio Valley and Great Lakes rides the westerlies as an open wave. It is a moderate-amplitude, three-trough/three-ridge longwave pattern that is progressive in the West and non-blocked overall — the eastern anticyclone is a ridge, not a Rex block, with no cutoff stacked beneath it.

Today's focal points cluster where the northern jet meets warm-sector moisture. SPC carries a Slight Risk across the Upper Midwest as the northern-Plains shortwave ejects and fires supercells along a cold front from far northeast South Dakota into western Minnesota this evening, with isolated 2-inch-plus hail, damaging winds, and a couple of tornadoes before convection clusters. A separate heavy-rain axis runs from the Lower Mississippi Valley through the Mid-Atlantic, with WPC flagging flash-flood risk near the Central Appalachians and the I-95 Philadelphia-Washington corridor; the Air Mass RGB confirms bright deep convective towers over the Louisiana-Mississippi Gulf Coast and a more organized cluster near the Georgia-Alabama border along the southern edge of the dry-moist boundary. Underneath the southern ridge, the Southern Plains bake toward daily-record upper-90s to triple-digit heat as the weakening Ohio Valley-to-Southern Plains stationary front retreats, while a second Pacific system arrives in the Northwest late Saturday with soaking Northern Rockies rain and temperatures 15-20 degrees below normal — the sharpest thermal contrast on the map.

The upper-level context ties this together and sets up the week. The broad orange-red airmass over the western and central CONUS is warm-season, low-PV subsidence air under the ridge — its spatial extent argues against a stratospheric read — but the full-disk imagery does show a compact, elongated high-PV stratospheric-intrusion signature on the cyclonic side of the flow over the central and northern Canadian Rockies, tied to the digging trough there. That intrusion is the leading edge of the real question. The prior several Tlaloc analyses framed the pattern as a heat ridge contracting south into a durable anchor; today's ensemble pair sharpens that into something more pointed for the northern interior. The 6-10 day height outlook shows only a modest western positive anomaly that does not penetrate east of the Rockies, dominated instead by a deep polar low over the Canadian Arctic Archipelago dropping a trough into the upper Great Lakes. By 8-14 days that trough deepens and takes over the north-central continent, and — critically — the positive anomaly retreats offshore to the northeastern Pacific and Alaska rather than rebuilding over western Canada or the northern Rockies. Comparing the two charts directly: the interior ridge does not regenerate poleward; it withdraws to the coast while the southern-tier heights stay high. SPC's Day 2 discussion says the same thing in plain language — attempts at building ridging across the northern Rockies and adjacent Plains "will be suppressed" by the digging border-vicinity shortwave, while subtropical ridging stays prominent across the central and southern Plains. So this is genuine geographic contraction, not cosmetic flattening: the north-central continent trends trough-dominant while the heat anchor holds in the south.
synthesis.climate_context: ENSO remains a strong El Niño, with the ONI reaching roughly +1.80 for June-August 2026 after a steady, reversal-free warming out of last winter's weak La Niña. The tropics fit that state: the Atlantic, Caribbean, and Gulf are shut down at what is climatologically near the season's peak, with NHC expecting no development for seven days, against a busy East Pacific — Tropical Storm Norbert west-southwest of Baja, a low development chance southeast of Hawaii, and a broad low southwest of Mexico given an 80 percent chance of becoming a depression late this weekend into early next week. That basin split is a textbook El Niño signature. Seasonally, the North American Monsoon stays active over the Southwest and interior Mexico, and late-summer severe weather is running in its expected ridge-periphery and frontal mode along the northern tier rather than as deep-Plains outbreaks. Teleconnections are a weak-season cross-check only and should not carry the story: a modestly negative PNA fits the eastern-side troughing, a near-zero AO offers little blocking support, and a notably negative NAO (7-day mean near -1.01) is consistent with the retarded downstream flow behind the retrogressive eastern ridge — but today's narrative rests on the height and PV fields, not the indices.
synthesis.regional_notes: SPC has no active mesoscale discussions. Today's immediate item is the Upper Midwest Slight Risk this evening — supercells from far northeast South Dakota into western Minnesota with isolated large hail, damaging winds, and a tornado risk before upscale growth — with a lower-confidence secondary threat over southern Nebraska into northern Kansas. The severe focus then shifts south Saturday to a Marginal Risk over the lower Missouri Valley (southeast Nebraska, southwest Iowa, northeast Kansas, north-central Missouri), where 2000-3000+ J/kg CAPE beneath an elevated mixed-layer plume could support isolated supercells and a possible evening cluster. Flash-flood sensitivity runs highest near the Central Appalachians and the Philadelphia-to-D.C. I-95 corridor, and the Southwest monsoon continues with isolated flash-flooding over burn scars and slot canyons. In Canada, a broad Prairie-through-Quebec high keeps light gradients over the continental interior, while an 986 hPa low with a well-developed frontal system off the Maritimes holds the tightest Canadian gradient; the digging shortwave near Hudson Bay is the feature to watch as it spins up renewed cyclogenesis over northern Quebec this weekend.

sources.title: Surface Analysis
sources.summary: This 1200Z 11 September 2026 WPC surface analysis shows a complex multi-center low pressure region across the Pacific Northwest and northern Rockies, with several L centers clustered between roughly 1000 and 1013 mb, the tightest being near the Washington-Oregon coast area around 1000-1006 mb. A sharp cold front extends southward from that low complex through the central Rockies into the Desert Southwest, with an associated warm front trailing eastward across the northern Plains; the cold frontal segment over the Southwest shows a tight pressure gradient with isobars packed closely, consistent with an active wind field there. Across the eastern two-thirds of the country the gradient is slack, with a diffuse surface low near 1000 mb over the central Plains and a sprawling surface trough extending into the Mississippi Valley where warm, moist surface air is evident from dew points in the upper 60s to mid-70s F; this trough and the moisture pooling along it are where surface-based lift is most favored, though the upper pattern would need to be consulted to assess convective potential. A broad high centered near 1020 mb sits over the Great Lakes region, and a second high of similar strength is positioned off the Southeast coast, with the corridor between them providing southerly low-level flow that is channeling Gulf moisture northward into the Gulf States and lower Mississippi Valley, where dew points reaching the upper 70s F are notable. The Atlantic and Gulf coastal regions show the slackest gradient on the chart, while the Pacific Northwest frontal zone and the Desert Southwest cold front retain the most organized isobar packing.

sources.title: Canadian Surface Analysis
sources.summary: This CMC surface analysis valid 0000Z Friday 11 September 2026 shows a dominant anticyclone centered near 1043 hPa positioned over the central North Pacific, with its influence extending northeastward toward the Alaska-Yukon region where a broad 1028 hPa high is plotted in what appears to be the interior Alaska or southwestern Yukon area based on the coastline geometry visible at left. A sprawling high pressure regime covers much of continental Canada from the Prairies eastward through Ontario and Quebec, with isobars spaced broadly enough to suggest light gradient winds across that swath, broken by a weak low near 994 hPa over what appears to be the northern Plains or Saskatchewan region and an associated frontal boundary trailing southward into the central United States. Along the eastern seaboard and into the western Atlantic, a low near 986 hPa with a well-developed frontal system — a cold front sweeping southwestward and a warm front arcing northward — is positioned off the coast near the Maritimes or just offshore, creating the tightest pressure gradient on the Canadian side of the chart in that corridor. Tropical Storm Lowell is explicitly labeled at 29N 169.5W, well out in the central North Pacific and posing no near-term threat to the continent. The upper portion of the frame, where several lows including centers near 979 and 990 hPa appear, represents the high Arctic and sub-Arctic ocean rather than populated Canadian provinces, and those systems should not be read as affecting the provinces without further analysis.

sources.title: 500 mb Analysis
sources.summary: At 0 UTC 11 September 2026 the 500 mb pattern shows a classic three-trough three-ridge longwave configuration across the CONUS domain. A deep, positively tilted trough is centered over the Pacific Northwest into British Columbia, with heights near 564 dam along its axis; the contours on its eastern flank are tightly packed over the Intermountain West, implying a strong implied jet corridor running from the northern Rockies toward the central Plains. A second, broad ridge occupies the central and southern Plains into the upper Midwest with heights reaching 588-591 dam, while a well-defined eastern ridge axis extending from the Carolinas northeastward into Atlantic Canada shows heights of 588-594 dam, consistent with the marked H symbol offshore the Mid-Atlantic. Between these ridges, a shortwave trough is evident over the Ohio Valley and Great Lakes region, oriented with a slight negative tilt, with heights near 580-582 dam; this feature appears to be an open wave still embedded in the westerlies rather than a closed low, as no enclosed height contour is evident around it. The western trough is the most amplified feature and shows no closed contour either, keeping the overall pattern progressive in the West while the eastern ridge appears more retrogressive, producing a moderate-amplitude but non-blocked pattern overall with roughly 25-30 dam of ridge-to-trough amplitude across the domain.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB (GOES-19)
sources.summary: At 1321Z on 11 September 2026, a broad orange-red airmass signature dominates the western third of the domain from the northern Plains southward through the central and southern Rockies into northern Mexico, consistent with dry upper-tropospheric air under an anticyclonic regime rather than a stratospheric intrusion given its spatial extent and ridge-flank position. A sharper, more elongated dry streamer arcs from the central Great Plains southeastward across the mid-Mississippi Valley and into the Tennessee Valley, where its leading edge meets the tropical green airmass to the east; this boundary is the likely jet corridor, with the implied flow running from the southwest toward the northeast. Scattered bright white deep convective towers are visible over the lower Mississippi Valley, the Gulf Coast states near Louisiana and Mississippi, and in a more organized cluster over the interior Southeast near the Georgia-Alabama border, all embedded within or along the southern margin of that dry-moist boundary. The northeastern quadrant of the domain from the Mid-Atlantic northward into southern New England shows a banded green-and-white cloud signature consistent with a frontal or baroclinic cloud shield, with additional convective cells visible offshore near the Carolina coast. The Caribbean and Gulf of Mexico portions of the domain appear largely green with modest low-to-mid cloud activity and no obvious organized tropical convective signature.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB Full Disk (GOES-19)
sources.summary: This GOES-19 AirMass RGB from 1320Z 11 September 2026 shows a broad tropical moist airmass (green) dominating from the eastern Pacific through the Caribbean and into northern South America, with scattered clusters of bright white deep convective tops along what appears to be the ITCZ over the eastern Pacific west of Central America and across equatorial South America near the Colombia-Ecuador border. A compact, well-organized convective system is visible over the western Caribbean and the Yucatan area, worth monitoring given the active late-season tropical environment. The Southern Hemisphere extratropics show a vigorous baroclinic zone across the far southern cone of South America and into the South Atlantic, with classic red-orange dry upper air on the poleward flank of the subtropical ridge over the South Atlantic and a curved cloud band consistent with a mature extratropical cyclone south of Argentina near 50-55 S. Across Canada and the northern tier of North America the airmass transitions sharply from the moist green tropical air to the deep blue-purple of cold dry upper-tropospheric air across the Canadian prairies and into the Arctic, with the implied polar jet boundary lying roughly along the U.S.-Canada border region. A streaky red-orange signature over the central and northern Canadian Rockies into the Great Plains appears compact and elongated on the cyclonic side of the flow, consistent with a stratospheric-intrusion signature associated with a trough or short-wave feature there.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day Temperature Outlook
sources.summary: The most striking feature is a broad above-normal signal spanning the entire western contiguous US, with the highest probabilities, 80-90%, centered over the interior Southwest and Great Basin, and a secondary 80-90% corridor stretching across the Gulf Coast states from Texas through Florida and into the Carolinas. The Pacific Northwest coast and most of the Rockies fall in the 60-70% above-normal range, and the signal extends through the central Plains at 40-50%, fading toward near-normal across the upper Midwest. The only below-normal signal is confined to the upper Great Lakes region, where probabilities reach 50-60% below normal, suggesting a cool trough or southward cold-air displacement is implied over that limited area while the rest of the country remains under a warm regime. Alaska shows a widespread 60-70% above-normal signal across the mainland, while far western Alaska and the western Aleutians are near-normal to slightly below, and Hawaii carries a strong 80-90% above-normal signal on the Big Island. The geographic split — strong warm probabilities anchored in the Southwest and Southeast simultaneously, with only a modest cool pocket over the Great Lakes — is consistent with a persistent ridge-dominated pattern over the western and southern US rather than a progressive breakdown, though the chart itself does not plot the upper-level wind field directly.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This chart is a 6-10 day 500 mb height and height-anomaly forecast valid 16-20 September 2026, made 10 September 2026, with green solid contours showing heights at 60 m intervals and dashed contours showing anomalies (blue negative, red positive, purple near-zero).

The dominant feature is a strong negative height anomaly centered over the Canadian Arctic Archipelago and Baffin Island, where the blue dashed contours reach their innermost closed values and the absolute heights fall to around 552 dam or below over the low center; this anomaly appears to be on the order of 6-9 dam below normal based on the number of blue contour rings visible. The trough axis associated with this cutoff-like low drops southward through Hudson Bay and into the upper Great Lakes region, with the absolute height contours tightly packed there and implying a brisk northwesterly flow across eastern Canada and the northeastern United States. Over the western contiguous United States and the eastern Pacific, the red dashed anomaly contours indicate a modest positive anomaly, perhaps 3-6 dam above normal, consistent with a broad ridge, but the zero-anomaly line (where purple dashed contours cross) appears to extend inland only to roughly the Rockies or just east of the Pacific Coast, suggesting the positive anomaly is not deeply penetrating the continent and the western ridge is not strongly amplified. The 582-588 dam height contours arch well into the central and southern United States, consistent with late-summer climatology, but the overall pattern with a deep polar trough dominating central and eastern Canada and only a weak western ridge implies the flow is trending toward an amplified trough-dominant pattern rather than becoming more zonal.

sources.title: CPC 8-14 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This chart is not a height-anomaly product. It plots 500 mb geopotential heights (solid green contours, 60 m interval) and what appear to be departure-from-normal contours (dashed, with blue dashed lines labeled in single-digit to low-double-digit values and red dashed lines similarly labeled), valid 18-24 September 2026 as an 8-14 day ensemble-mean outlook made 10 September 2026.

The dominant feature is a deep, closed cyclonic circulation centered over the central Canadian Arctic, with the innermost height contour near 5460 dam and concentric rings expanding outward. The trough axis extends southward from that center into the north-central United States, with the 5580-5640 dam contours bowing well southward across the central Plains, placing unseasonably low heights across the northern and central interior of the continent.

Regarding the key question about western Canada and the northern Rockies: the height contours over that region run nearly meridionally and show no ridge axis or amplified ridge core there. Instead, the ridge implied by the poleward-bowing contours lies well to the west, over the northeastern Pacific and the Alaska-British Columbia coast, while the southern United States shows relatively higher heights (5760-5880 dam range across the Desert Southwest and Gulf Coast latitudes), consistent with a positively anomalous area there. The blue dashed anomaly contours (positive departure) are centered over roughly the northeastern Pacific and into Alaska, while negative anomaly contours (red dashed) surround the Canadian Arctic low and extend into the central continent. There is no evidence in this chart of a positive height anomaly over western Canada, the northern Rockies, or the northern Plains; the ridge core has not extended into those areas, and the pattern instead favors a persistent trough over the north-central continent for that period.

sources.title: WPC Short Range Forecast Discussion
sources.summary: Stationary front from Ohio Valley to Southern Plains will weaken this weekend as warmth returns; potential daily high temperature records in Southern Plains with upper-90s to triple-digit heat. Broad area of showers and thunderstorms expected Lower Mississippi Valley through Mid-Atlantic, with isolated to scattered heavy rainfall and flash flooding risk, particularly near Central Appalachians and I-95 corridor Philadelphia-Washington D.C. Northern Tier active with two Pacific systems; scattered heavy rain and severe weather possible Upper Mississippi Valley/Upper Midwest this afternoon along lead cold front. Rainfall focus shifts south toward Central Plains weekend. Second system arrives Northwest late Saturday with soaking rains through Northern Rockies; mixed precipitation possible Sunday morning with temperatures 15-20 degrees below normal. Southwest monsoon thunderstorms continue with isolated flash flooding potential, especially over burn scars and slot canyons.

sources.title: SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook
sources.summary: Upper Midwest experiencing a Slight Risk of severe thunderstorms late afternoon into tonight. A mid-level shortwave trough ejecting eastward over the northern Plains will spawn organized convection along a surface cold front across far northeast South Dakota into western Minnesota by 22-01Z. Large hail (isolated 2+ inches), damaging winds, and a couple of tornadoes possible with initial supercells, though convective mode expected to trend toward clustering. Severe wind threat diminishes eastward into Minnesota and Wisconsin by late evening. South Dakota into central Plains convection highly uncertain but could support severe hail/wind if storms develop, particularly southern Nebraska into northern Kansas. Southeast features also promoting disorganized convection across Mid-South, Tennessee Valley, and Carolinas with occasional damaging wind threat.

sources.title: SPC Mesoscale Discussions
sources.summary: No active mesoscale convective threat is currently being monitored by SPC. No discussions have been issued in the past six hours.

sources.title: NHC Tropical Weather Outlooks
sources.summary:
Atlantic: No tropical cyclone formation expected over the next 7 days across the Atlantic, Caribbean, or Gulf of America.

East Pacific: Tropical Storm Norbert is under advisory west-southwest of Baja California. A disorganized system southeast of Hawaii shows low development potential (20 percent through 7 days), moving generally northward. A broad low pressure area southwest of Mexico has higher development prospects—gradual organization anticipated with tropical depression formation likely late weekend or early next week as the system tracks west-northwestward; 80 percent formation chance through 7 days.

sources.title: ENSO State (Oceanic Niño Index)
sources.summary: The Oceanic Niño Index shows a transition from weak La Niña conditions (anomaly -0.60 in NDJ 2025) toward El Niño. Cold anomalies persist through early 2026 but diminish rapidly. By spring 2026, anomalies turn positive and strengthen substantially, reaching +1.80 by summer 2026 (JJA). The index itself rises from 25.96 to 29.09 across the period. This trajectory indicates a pronounced shift toward warm ENSO conditions developing through the first half of 2026.

sources.title: Teleconnection Indices (PNA, AO, NAO)
sources.summary: PNA remains negative around -0.34 with little recent change, supporting eastern trough/western ridge positioning but weak and not canonical for August. AO has rebounded to +0.53 after dipping negative mid-period, now near zero on the 7-day mean—no strong high-latitude blocking signal. NAO has fallen notably to -1.01 on the 7-day mean and stands at -0.66, trending increasingly negative over the past week. Negative NAO favors Atlantic blocking patterns that could trap eastern cutoffs rather than allowing escape downstream.
